chunks: Abu al-Husayn Muhammad ibn Harun al-Zanjani told us, saying: Ali ibn Abd al-Aziz narrated to us from al-Qasim ibn Salam

He said: The 'ajma' is the beast, and it was named 'ajma' because it does not speak, and everyone who is unable to speak is 'ajam' and 'musta'jam'. From this is the saying of al-Hasan (peace be upon him): 'The daytime prayer is 'ajma,' meaning recitation is not heard in it. As for 'jubar', it is 'hadr' (liability without compensation). The wound of the beast is only considered 'hadr' if it is loose, having no leader, no driver, and no rider. If one of these three is with it, he is a guarantor, because the liability at that time is not for the beast, but for its owner who allowed people to ride it. As for his saying: 'And the well is jubar,' there is more than one saying. It is said: It refers to a well whose owner hires a man to dig it in his property, and it collapses on the digger; hence, there is no liability upon its owner. It is also said: It is a well that is in a man's ownership, and a human or an animal falls into it; hence, there is no liability upon him, because it is in his ownership.
ai.seo_question: What is the legal definition of 'jubar' and 'ajma' in Shia fiqh regarding animal and well liability?
ai.summary: Shaykh al-Saduq elucidates the jurisprudential distinctions between 'ajma' (non-speaking beasts) and 'jubar' (strict liability), clarifying that animal injuries are uncompensated ('hadr') only when the beast is uncontrolled, whereas the owner bears responsibility otherwise. The text further debates the legal status of wells, distinguishing between scenarios where the owner is exempt from liability due to the well's inherent nature or hired labor versus cases of personal possession, reflecting the nuanced Shia approach to property rights and accidental damage.
